Question: Lime (CaO) is made by heating limestone (CaCO₃) in a kiln. At room temperature limestone lasts for centuries; in the kiln, a CO₂ sensor at the flue climbs as the stone decomposes. CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ has ΔH° > 0 and ΔS° > 0. Why does heating turn the reaction on?
Answer: Appendix G: ΔH° = +191.6 kJ, ΔS° = +141.9 J/K (gas formed). ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°: +149.3 kJ at 298 K; zero at T = ΔH° ÷ ΔS° = 1350 K; −21.3 kJ at 1500 K. With both positive, the −TΔS° term overcomes ΔH° only at high T.
Target concept: When ΔH° and ΔS° are both positive, the reaction becomes spontaneous above T = ΔH° ÷ ΔS°.

Question: The Haber-Bosch reactor makes ammonia, N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, a reaction with ΔH° < 0 and ΔS° < 0. Engineers would like it cold, yet must run it hot, and a thermodynamic table sets a temperature limit. What happens to the sign of ΔG° as the reactor heats up, and why?
Answer: ΔH° = −91.8 kJ, ΔS° = −198.1 J/K: ΔG° < 0 only below T = ΔH° ÷ ΔS° = 463 K. Above it, the −TΔS° term (positive) outweighs ΔH°: ΔG° = +46.9 kJ at 700 K. Industry runs hot for speed, at high pressure to compensate.
Target concept: When ΔH° and ΔS° are both negative, the reaction is spontaneous only below T = ΔH° ÷ ΔS°.

Question: Hydrogen peroxide in a brown bottle slowly breaks down into water and oxygen at any temperature, and an oxygen sensor in the cap finds O₂ building up month by month. Ozone, by contrast, never forms from oxygen on its own. Which sign combinations of ΔH° and ΔS° make a reaction spontaneous at every temperature, or at none?
Answer: 2H₂O₂(l) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂: ΔH° = −196.1 kJ, ΔS° = +126.0 J/K: ΔG° < 0 at all T (always). 3O₂ → 2O₃: ΔH° = +285.4 kJ, ΔS° = −137.8 J/K: ΔG° > 0 at all T (never). When ΔH and ΔS push ΔG the same way, temperature cannot flip the sign.
Target concept: ΔH < 0 with ΔS > 0 is spontaneous at all temperatures; ΔH > 0 with ΔS < 0 at none.

Question: Iron is smelted by heating iron ore with carbon: Fe₂O₃ + 3C → 2Fe + 3CO. At room temperature the mixture just sits; in a furnace, a CO sensor at the top shows the gas pouring out. Both ΔH° and ΔS° are positive. Above what temperature does the reaction become spontaneous, and why?
Answer: ΔH° = +492.6 kJ, ΔS° = +543.1 J/K (three moles of gas formed): T = ΔH° ÷ ΔS° = 907 K. Below it ΔG° > 0 (+330.8 kJ at 298 K); above it ΔG° < 0 (−159.1 kJ at 1200 K). The entropy of the CO gas, multiplied by a high T, drives the reaction.
Target concept: High temperature drives reactions with positive ΔH° and positive ΔS°.
